Coastal towns brace for record spring tides

By Jane MarlowEnvironment correspondent
25 September 2026

Residents of low-lying coastal towns spent the weekend filling sandbags as forecasters warned that this week's spring tides could be the highest recorded in more than twenty years.

The combination of a new moon, a low-pressure system moving in from the Atlantic and strong onshore winds is expected to push water levels well above normal on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings.

"We have been preparing for this for months," said harbour master Tom Reilly, standing on the sea wall as waves broke over the lower promenade. "The defences were upgraded after the last big surge, but nobody wants to find out the hard way whether they are high enough."

The Environment Agency has issued seventeen flood warnings along the coast, and temporary barriers have been installed at four points where the permanent walls are still under construction.

Local councils have opened rest centres in schools and community halls, and have asked people living closest to the shore to make plans to stay with friends or relatives on higher ground if the warnings are upgraded.

Scientists say events like this are becoming more frequent as sea levels rise. Average sea level around the coast has risen by about sixteen centimetres since 1900, and the rate of rise has roughly doubled in the last thirty years.

Insurers have urged homeowners to check their policies and to photograph the contents of ground-floor rooms before the high tides arrive, to make any claims easier to process.

The highest tide is forecast for 19:42 on Wednesday. Forecasters will update their warnings twice daily until the risk has passed.
